messages.subject: Re: Comparing densities from different areas
messages.subject_clean: Comparing densities from different areas
messages.body_plain:
Julie:

There are several problems with your approach.  Unless you have an
immense number of transects (>30) you won't be able to establish the
normality (or lack thereof) of the estimates produced from each.  And I
don't think there is a reason to determine the normality of that
distribution.

Your transects are not independent replicates because you are using the
same detection function for each transect within one of your areas.
Because they share the same detection function (or f-hat(0) if you
wish), they will have a covariance between them, so you ought not use
them as replicates.

You would be better served to use an analysis method described in
Buckland, S.T., Russell, R.E., Dickson, B.G., Saab, V.A., Gorman, D.G.
and Block, W.M. 2009.  Analysing designed experiments in distance
sampling.  Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental
Statistics 14, 432-442.
<http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/buckland%20et%20al%20jabes%202009.pdf>
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/buckland%20et%20al%20jabes%202009.pdf

Regarding the faeces analysis, you indeed cannot use distance sampling
if there are no measured distances.  You will have count data unadjusted
for detectability so you will have to rely upon the untestable
assumption that detectability is unchanging among your study areas.
That is a much more unlikely assumption than anything you might want to
demonstrate regarding normality.

messages.subject_clean: Detection probability and survey timing
messages.body_plain:
Dear DISTANCErs,

We=92ve just completed line-transect surveys for large ungulates in the
Eastern Plains Landscape of Cambodia. Surveys were timed for the season

(late Jan through May) when visibility (and hence probably detectability of

focal species) is greatest following the burning of the deciduous

dipterocarp forest which removes most of the grass understorey. Despite a
lot of effort (>500-km of >60 transects) the number of encounters of some
focal species is low (e.g. <35 encounters of Banteng and Eurasian Wild Pig)=
.
Therefore we are planning to re-survey all transects once in the 2010/2011

dry-season (an additional 250-km) to increase sample size.

My question regards the timing of these surveys. Is it sensible to begin

these surveys in November, when the sites become accessible after the

wet-season but prior to burning, and therefore visibility/detectability of
focal species may be lower (due to higher grass) or should we wait until

late-Jan to coincide the timing surveys with those from the 2009/10? If

detection varies between surveys is this likely to be a major problem in th=

e
analysis (intuitively it would seem to be so but some advice would be
appreciated)

Thanks

Tom Gray

messages.body_plain:
Tom:

By changing the timing of your survey you will increase the likelihood=20
that your detection function will differ between surveys; but even=20
keeping your surveys consistent just after the burning season does not=20
guarantee you will have constant detection functions.

Note, I am treating the term 'survey' as a period during which you wish=20
to produce an abundance estimate.  I'm not certain from the context of=20
your question whether you are contemplating extending the duration of=20
your survey to encompass both the post-burn season as well as the=20
dry-season and merging all of the data collected into a single=20
population estimate.  That will be challenging fundamentally from a=20
biological standpoint; over what duration are you willing to assume=20
constancy of the population you are studying?

If on the other hand, you wish to perform a survey during the post-burn=20
period and a second survey during the dry season, and compare your=20
findings, then you need not be concerned about differences in detection=20
functions between surveys because that will be accommodated in your=20
analysis.

Steer me back in the right direction if I have misunderstood your questio=
n.

id layer, and begin designing the survey. You could use the stratum layer fo=
r the design and then you can do things like orient the lines independently i=

messages.subject_clean: analyzing density vs. counts with trapping web data
messages.body_plain:
I have small mammal trapping web data from a designed experiment with 12=20
stands divided into control stands (3), and 3 fuel-reduction treatments,=20
each with 2-4 replicates.  Each stand had one trapping web.  I analyzed 2=20
species with good data: deer mice and yellow-pine chipmunks.  Captures in=20
each of the 4 treatment ?strata? were insufficient for estimating separate =

detection functions, so I estimated a global detection function for each=20
species to estimate density in each treatment unit.=20

Each species has  about 100 total detections, but the density estimate for =

deer mice was 15/ha whereas for chipmunks was 40/ha.  I assume this is=20
because the detection functions differ, hence the density estimates=20
differ.  Reviewers suspect a fatal flaw here,  and suggest I simply use=20
the counts of individuals for each web in ANOVA, especially since I used a =

global detection function.  Two questions:

Could you comment on the disparity between the density estimates between=20
the species given similar number of captures, i.e. am I correct in my=20
interpretation?=20

Is it correct to use the simple count data from the webs vs. the Distance=20
estimates?  My guess is no.

I did an ANOVA of the density estimates, but understand there is the=20
covariance issue with the global detection function.  I will investigate=20
Buckland?s methods for designed experiments, if that is your=20
recommendation and you do not recommend ANOVA of simple counts.  Thanks.

messages.subject_clean: Frequency scaling in point transect histograms
messages.body_plain:
Hi list,

This is my first time posting on here, please forgive me if this question
has been previously posted - I have searched through the archive and
couldn't spot anything related though.

My question is regarding how the histogram of detection data is scaled in
point transects to correct for the increasing area surveyed with distance
away from the point.  I have been running some MCDS analyses as I am
interested in potential differences in detection probability (p) among
factor levels (such as habitat), and for this have R code for different
detection functions allowing me to use integrate() to calculate p for each
level (as suggested in the Distance 6.0 help).  I realise the easiest option
for plotting the histograms is probably to output DistancePlot files, but
given that I have code for the detection function, I figured it would be
easy enough to add this to the histogram of data for each factor level
within R.  However, I am having trouble reproducing the histogram data at
the correct scale outside of Distance, and a bit of digging in Buckland et
al. (2001) and online made me realise that it is unclear (to me) exactly how
the rescaling of frequencies for point transects is performed within
Distance.  I hope someone is able to help me out, there is probably an
obvious answer I have missed (if so, please do take this off-list).

To highlight my lack of understanding in an example that can hopefully be
easily followed by all, I've used the point transect example from Buckland
et al. (2001:149) with data truncated at 20m shown in Fig. 5.2 (data found
in the Distance Sample Project called 'Point Transect Example').  I follow
that each detection distance r[i] is assigned a weight 1/r[i], with the sum
of these weights across observations within a distance interval being the
scaled frequencies for each interval.  However, I don't follow how to arrive
at the values in the histogram in Fig. 5.2a, as if I follow the previous
step by calculating weights and summing them within the distance intervals
in Fig. 5.2 I get a histogram with quite different values.  I am missing a
scaling step somewhere, but I don't know what it is.  Please find the R code
I have used to illustrate this below, I look forward to hearing from someone
before I lose all of my hair!

Many thanks,
Tom

Tom Porteus
PhD Candidate
Department of Zoology, University of British Columbia
por...@zoology.ubc.ca

#point_example.txt is the data from this Distance sample project copied from
the clipboard
dist.data <- read.table("point_example_data.txt",sep="\t",skip=5,header=F)
#select distance column and truncate at 20m
w <- 20
dist.m <- as.numeric(subset(dist.data, V10<=w, select=V10)[,1])
#set histogram bins as in Fig. 5.2(b) of Buckland et al (2001) for data
visualisation
breaks <- c(0,4,8,12,16,20)
point.hist <- hist(dist.m, breaks=breaks, labels=T, freq=T,
			xlab="radial detection distance (m)")
#calculate weights for individual detection distances
weight.r <- 1/dist.m
dist.wt.matrix <- cbind(dist.m, weight.r)
#split distances into intervals and sum weights - these should equal scaled
frequencies of Fig. 5.2(a)
wt1 <- subset(dist.wt.matrix,dist.wt.matrix[,1]>=0 & dist.wt.matrix[,1]<=4);
wt1sum <- sum(wt1[,2])
wt2 <- subset(dist.wt.matrix,dist.wt.matrix[,1]>4 & dist.wt.matrix[,1]<=8);
wt2sum <- sum(wt2[,2])
wt3 <- subset(dist.wt.matrix,dist.wt.matrix[,1]>8 & dist.wt.matrix[,1]<=12);
wt3sum <- sum(wt3[,2])
wt4 <- subset(dist.wt.matrix,dist.wt.matrix[,1]>12 &
dist.wt.matrix[,1]<=16); wt4sum <- sum(wt4[,2])
wt5 <- subset(dist.wt.matrix,dist.wt.matrix[,1]>16 &
dist.wt.matrix[,1]<=20); wt5sum <- sum(wt5[,2])
calc.scaled.freq <- c(wt1sum, wt2sum, wt3sum, wt4sum, wt5sum)
#approx weights if use frequency form of data with these intervals
approx.wts <- 1/point.hist$mids
approx.scaled.freq <- approx.wts * point.hist$counts
#calc and approx frequencies are similar as expected
print(calc.scaled.freq)	#[1] 4.683044 4.664788 3.511822 2.816054 1.287087
print(approx.scaled.freq)	#[1] 4.500000 4.333333 3.400000 2.785714
1.277778

Distance model of ungrouped data

print(D6.scaled.freq)

messages.subject_clean: Frequency scaling in point transect histograms
messages.body_plain:
Tom, I believe we revised how this is done in Distance at some point.
What is done is explained on p150 of the 2001 book.  The weighting by
1/p_i in the current version is done indirectly.  We simply take for a
given interval the number of animals detected, and divide this by the
area surveyed for that interval, which is k times (area of circle of
radius s) times (area of circle of radius r), where k is number of
points, and the interval runs from distance r to distance s from the
point.  We then divide this apparent density by the estimated density
from Distance - 79.6 in this example.  This approach overcomes a few
difficulties with the earlier approach, such as what to do if you have a
zero distance.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: analyzing density vs. counts with trapping web data
messages.body_plain:
John, I would have thought that the disparity in density estimates was
proof, if any was needed, that you can't simply do an ANOVA on counts.
There clearly is a difference in trappability, so counts across species
are not comparable.  There are other problems with trapping webs (e.g.
you must assume animals at the centre are certain to be trapped;  it's
fairly critical to get the trap spacing right relative to home range
size;  and they're very labour-intensive if you are to have reasonable
replication).  We've been working on an alternative - trapping point
transects - for that reason.  These do not assume certain detection at
the point, and require far fewer traps to be set.  See J Appl Ecol 43,
377-384 (2006).  The method works well if there isn't a strong response
to trapping.  A research student of ours, Joanne Potts, has been
developing the method for use on woodrats.

Yes, the methods we used for analysis of designed experiments in
distance sampling (JABES 14, 432-442, 2009) should work OK.  Cornelia
Oedekoven, a research student of ours, is also working on an integrated
approach, which we hope might be better than this 2-stage approach, but
we're not quite there yet.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Florian:

Encounter rate only makes sense at the stratum level, which is why
Distance does not show it to you at the global level if you have
performed a stratified analysis.  If you did not presume that encounter
rate varied across your study area then you likely would not have
stratified your analysis.  If you would like to know the global
encounter rate, I think you could simply run your analysis without
stratification.  I'm not saying you should use the density/abundance
estimate produced therefrom, but if you have curiosity about the global
encounter rate, you can obtain that statistic by performing your
analysis without stratification.

messages.subject: Re: Computing global encounter rate
messages.subject_clean: Computing global encounter rate
messages.body_plain:
Adding to what Eric said, it depends on the reason why you want a global
rate.  I've not come across an example where it is a sensible thing to
calculate, but it is easy to calculate.  Eric's suggestion of ignoring
stratification is the simple solution, and effectively weights by line
length in each stratum.  Depending on the purpose, you might prefer to
weight by stratum area.  You can get this by taking a weighted average
of the stratum encounter rates, with weights proportional to area.
Because encounter rate is independently estimated in each stratum, there
are no covariances, so finding the variance of the weighted average is
straightforward - evaluate weight squared times variance of e.r. for
each stratum, then sum these.  Take square root for std error, and
divide by the average encounter rate for cv.  (This assumes weights are
normalised, so they sum to one.)

Steve Buckland

Nicole:

We placed checks inside the DSM package to ensure that all detected
objects used in the DSM analysis had associated detection probabilities
from previous fittings of ddf() that resides in the MRDS package.  We
did that by checking that the same filter was used both for fitting the
detection function and fitting the density surface.  I suspect that is
the check of which you are running afoul when trying to use the global
detection function to apply to sightings only from the northern study area.

One way to accomplish what you wish, is to do a little 'mining' inside
the R workspace created by Distance.  Fit a global detection function to
all of your data using ddf().  Having done so, you will have a object
called ddf.x (where x is a number corresponding to the analysis you have
run).  You can then examine the contents of that object in which you
will be able to find a detection probability estimated for all detected
objects in your survey.  You may access these detection probabilities
for the northern region, and insert the detection probabilities into a
Distance project that contains the survey information associated with
the northern region.

Notice the Model Definition Properties window associated with the DSM
engine where you specify the density surface model you wish to fit.
Look at the top right portion of the window, you will see a section for
'Detection probabilities.'  Most commonly, you select the fitted
function that you used to estimate the detection function.  However, you
may also choose 'table of values' in which case you are asked to choose
a field from the observation layer that contains the detection
probability associated with the detected objects.

It is through that mechanism that you can specify detection
probabilities for your northern region that you have derived from
fitting a detection function to all of your observations throughout your
study area.

If you have questions about those steps, contact me off line for further
clarification.

John, I would have thought that the disparity in density estimates was
proof, if any was needed, that you can't simply do an ANOVA on counts.
There clearly is a difference in trappability, so counts across species
are not comparable.  There are other problems with trapping webs (e.g.
you must assume animals at the centre are certain to be trapped;  it's
fairly critical to get the trap spacing right relative to home range
size;  and they're very labour-intensive if you are to have reasonable
replication).  We've been working on an alternative - trapping point
transects - for that reason.  These do not assume certain detection at
the point, and require far fewer traps to be set.  See J Appl Ecol 43,
377-384 (2006).  The method works well if there isn't a strong response
to trapping.  A research student of ours, Joanne Potts, has been
developing the method for use on woodrats.

Yes, the methods we used for analysis of designed experiments in
distance sampling (JABES 14, 432-442, 2009) should work OK.  Cornelia
Oedekoven, a research student of ours, is also working on an integrated
approach, which we hope might be better than this 2-stage approach, but
we're not quite there yet.

Steve Buckland
